--- Page 1 ---
Optimal Energy and LLM Task Scheduling for
Multiple Cloud Data Centers
Zhongqi Zhao∗†, Lei Fan∗†, and Zhu Han∗
∗Department of Electrical and Computer Engineering, University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA
†Department of Engineering Technology, University of Houston, Houston, TX, USA
Abstract—This paper studies coordinated Large Language
Model (LLM) training-task scheduling and facility operation
for geographically distributed cloud data centers (CDCs). The
central question is how two scheduling flexibilities—cross-CDC
task transfer and task reordering—affect service and economic
outcomes when remote execution remains subject to compute,
bandwidth, energy, and zone-temperature constraints. We formu-
late a mixed-integer optimization model that jointly determines
task outcomes, heterogeneous-node assignment, execution timing,
pre-execution data transfer, node activation, and facility opera-
tion. A deterministic 24-hour case study contains 3 CDCs, 15
heterogeneous graphics processing unit (GPU) nodes, 4 thermal
zones per CDC, and 103 tasks. In this instance, enabling transfer
increases net profit by 57.9% relative to the otherwise matched
no-transfer variant and increases completed tasks from 76 to 103.
The more restrictive no-transfer FIFO-prefix variant completes
14 tasks and yields negative profit. The proposed schedule trans-
fers 39 tasks, achieves 70.3% node utilization, and maintains zone
temperatures within 24◦C–27◦C. These fixed-instance results
indicate that cross-CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility
can improve the modeled profit and task-completion outcomes
under the studied conditions.
Index Terms—Cloud data centers, energy management, LLM
task scheduling, mixed-integer linear programming, optimization
I. INTRODUCTION
Training Large Language Models (LLMs) requires substan-
tial computation, data movement, and storage input/output
(I/O), and these workloads are commonly executed in cloud
data centers (CDCs) [1], [2]. In a geographically distributed
deployment, an operator must decide not only when and where
each training task runs, but also whether its data should be
transferred to another CDC. That placement decision changes
node use, communication demand, heat generation, and facility
energy requirements.
Prior work has addressed several parts of this problem.
Cooling-control and digital-twin methods target facility energy
[3], while learning-based approaches schedule or migrate data-
center tasks [4]. Recent studies also consider multi-cloud
task scheduling, data-center network management, and geo-
distributed job-and-data placement [5]–[7]. These advances
establish that geographic placement, communication, and fa-
cility operation matter. They do not, however, determine how
much value arises from cross-CDC transfer and how much
arises from relaxing a restrictive task order when both mech-
anisms are evaluated under the same physical and economic
constraints.
LLM training tasks are both computation- and data-
intensive. Their placement therefore cannot be based on pro-
cessor availability alone: a remote task consumes outbound
and inbound bandwidth, and its data must arrive before exe-
cution begins. CDCs also differ in node composition, avail-
able capacity, and operating conditions. A remote assignment
can improve the modeled objective only when its placement
benefit offsets transfer cost and remains feasible under these
constraints [7], [8].
Task placement is also coupled to facility operation. Ac-
tivating a node changes computing energy and zone heat,
which affects air-conditioning demand and the site energy
balance. Storage, renewable supply, and grid purchases further
constrain feasible operation. Carbon-aware scheduling across
AI data-center parks similarly shows that workload flexibility
must be interpreted together with site conditions [9]. Here,
these facility constraints provide the feasibility context for
comparing the two scheduling flexibilities; they are not treated
as an independent claim of universal energy efficiency.
Motivated by this distinction, we ask a question regard-
ing to a fixed time horizon: under one coupled compute–
communication–facility model, what changes when cross-
CDC transfer is disabled, and what changes when task re-
ordering is additionally replaced by a FIFO-prefix restriction?
The comparison is diagnostic rather than statistical. It separates
the two modeled flexibility mechanisms while holding the task
set, node set, CDC assignments, rewards, penalties, and energy
parameters fixed.
The main contributions of this paper are summarized as
follows:
• We
formulate
a
multi-CDC
optimization
model
that
couples
task
outcomes
and
execution
timing
with heterogeneous-node assignment and bandwidth-
constrained, pre-execution task transfer.
• We place these decisions within modeled node-energy,
zone-temperature, air-conditioning, storage, renewable-
supply,
and
grid-purchase
constraints
so
that
each
scheduling variant is evaluated under the same cross-layer
feasibility conditions.
• We use a fixed-instance comparison of the proposed, No
Transfer (No TF), and No Transfer with FIFO-prefix
order (No TF+FIFO) variants to separate the effects
of cross-CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility on
profit, task completion, concurrency, and node utilization.

The rest of this paper is organized as follows. Section II
presents the problem definition and mathematical formulation.
Section III reports the numerical results and discusses the
scheduling and energy-management behavior of the optimized
solution. Section IV concludes the paper.
II. PROBLEM DEFINITION AND FORMULATIONS
This section presents a mixed-integer programming (MIP)
formulation for net operating profit under LLM training-task
scheduling, data transfer, and facility constraints. We consider
a set I of CDCs located in different regions. Each task j ∈J
has a fixed home CDC denoted by hj ∈I. Tasks are classified
exogenously as non-time-sensitive (NTS), time-sensitive (TS),
or already running before the scheduling horizon. The TS
class represents users who selected priority service before
the optimization begins; priority purchase is not a decision
variable. Table I illustrates the initial task pools.
Each CDC contains heterogeneous computing nodes dis-
tributed across thermal zones. Let Ni,z be the nodes in zone
z of CDC i, and let ℓn ∈I denote the CDC containing node
n. Fig. 1 illustrates the resulting multi-CDC hierarchy and
the coupling between task transfer, zone-level computing, and
facility operation.
Given task classes, home CDCs, processing times, dead-
lines, data volumes, economic coefficients, node limits, and
facility profiles, the model determines each task outcome,
execution node and interval, required transfer, and CDC energy
dispatch. A remote assignment is feasible only when its data
reach the destination before startup and both CDCs satisfy
their communication limits. The output is therefore a joint
task, transfer, node, storage, HVAC, and grid schedule rather
than an unconstrained geographic placement.
A. Cloud Data Center Modeling Overview
We formulate the multi-CDC coordination problem over
t ∈T = {1, 2, . . . , T} with step length ∆t. The optimizer
jointly determines task status, execution node, running tra-
jectory, inter-CDC data transfer, battery charging/discharging,
HVAC operation, and grid purchase. Indices i, j, n, z, and
t denote CDC, task, node, zone, and time slot; sets I, J ,
N, Z, and T
collect them. Binary variables are mainly
{x, u, v, z, y}; other lowercase symbols denote continuous de-
cision variables. Uppercase symbols and Greek letters denote
parameters/constants, except temperature variables such as

execution assignment and temporal consistency, node-level
capacity coupling, and cross-CDC transfer feasibility.

C. Facility Energy and Zone-Temperature Constraints
We adapt the data-center energy model in [10]. For each
one-hour slot, the site energy balance is

Coefficients ai,z′,z and bi,z absorb the one-hour discretiza-

contribution only to its own zone and keeps the printed model
affine. The case study enforces the reported zone-temperature
bounds. The supplied result package does not document a
cyclic terminal battery condition, so the grid-purchase results
below are interpreted only for this 24-h instance.
III. NUMERICAL VALIDATION
We solve the deterministic case study with the commercial
solver Gurobi on a workstation.
A. Experimental Setup
The deterministic case includes 3 CDCs, 15 heterogeneous
GPU nodes, 103 LLM training tasks, and a 24-h horizon with
one-hour time slots. Each CDC has 4 thermal zones, and the
workload contains 72 NTS tasks, 30 TS tasks, and 1 already-
running task. Node types are listed in Table II. Idle power is
set to 20% of rated node power. Power is represented in kW;
under the one-hour case assumption, slot energy is in kWh
and cumulative energy is reported in MWh. The formulation
represents independently executable, single-node training jobs;
it does not model synchronized distributed training, checkpoint
failures, or communication collectives during execution. The
supplied package does not document measurement provenance
for every task and facility parameter, so the study is treated
as a parameterized case rather than a production trace.
We conduct three experiments using identical tasks, nodes,
CDC assignments, rewards, hold/abort penalties, transfer costs,
and energy parameters. The Proposed model retains cross-
CDC transfer and task-reordering flexibility. The No Transfer
(No TF) variant prohibits cross-CDC transfer while preserving
reordering. The No Transfer with FIFO-prefix order (No
TF+FIFO) variant additionally prevents a later task from
being selected when an earlier task in the same fixed order is
skipped. This restriction is stronger than a general operational
FIFO policy. Proposed versus No TF isolates cross-CDC
transfer within this model, whereas No TF versus No TF+FIFO
isolates relaxation of the implemented FIFO-prefix restriction.
Monetary quantities are reported in NMU, energy prices in
NMU/kWh, and transfer quantities in NDU or NDU/slot as
applicable. These same-instance comparisons are descriptive,
not statistical.
The Proposed case was solved with Gurobi 11.0.3 on an
AMD Ryzen 9 3900X using 24 threads. Before presolve,
the model contained 259,433 constraints, 231,097 variables,

returned an incumbent of 26,025.1126 NMU, a best bound
of 26,027.0789 NMU, and a 0.0076% relative gap under
the configured 10−4 tolerance. Equivalent terminal logs were
not available in the supplied package for the two restricted
variants; their results are therefore reported without a solver-
quality equivalence claim.
B. Comparative Results
1) Flexibility, Profit, and Completion: In this fixed instance,
Table III shows monotonic improvement as the two mod-
eled flexibilities are restored. Enabling cross-CDC transfer
increases profit from 16,483.81 to 26,025.11 NMU, a gain of
9,541.30 NMU or 57.9% relative to No TF, while completing
27 additional tasks. Relaxing the FIFO-prefix restriction has a
larger descriptive difference: No TF+FIFO completes 14 tasks
and yields negative profit because 30 TS tasks are aborted
and 59 NTS tasks are held, whereas No TF completes 76
tasks. The proposed model completes all 103 tasks without
aborting or holding any task. These comparisons quantify the
two flexibility effects for the stated formulation and instance;
they do not establish their distribution across other workloads.
2) Scheduling Behavior and Service Capability: Table IV
reports the associated scheduling behavior. The proposed
model sustains 10.54 concurrent tasks on average, compared
with 6.92 for No TF and 1.00 for No TF+FIFO. Its peak
task/computing-node concurrency reaches 11/11, and com-
pleted tasks are distributed as 45/23/35 across the three CDCs.
The optimized transfer of 320.62 normalized data units ac-
companies the increase in completed-task throughput rather
than merely changing execution locations. Although the mean
completion slots are similar across the variants, the proposed
model completes substantially more tasks within the same 24-
slot horizon.
3) Grid Energy, Server Activity, and Battery Operation:
Table V reports grid purchases, battery operation, and node
activity while excluding electricity-purchase cost. Despite
completing 27 more tasks, the proposed solution purchases
2.145 MWh from the grid, approximately 3.736 MWh (63.5%)
less than No TF based on the unrounded values. This is

a grid-purchase comparison, not a general energy-efficiency
result: the variants complete different numbers of tasks and
use storage differently.
Figure 3 compares stored-energy trajectories across the three
CDCs. The proposed trajectory declines from 158.5 kWh at
the first recorded slot to 37.5 kWh at the last recorded slot in
each CDC. Because the supplied package does not document
a cyclic terminal-storage requirement, part of the 24-h grid-
purchase outcome depends on using initially available stored
energy. No TF relies more heavily on CDC 0, whereas No
TF+FIFO combines low grid purchase with low activity. Its
zero grid purchase does not imply greater energy efficiency
because it completes only 14 tasks and activates computing
nodes in 6.7% of node-time slots.
4) Detailed Scheduling and Node Selection:
Figure 2
presents the proposed task schedule, where jp, tjp, and wj
denote NTS, TS, and already-running tasks. The implemented
inventory contains the five node types in Table II. DGXH100,
DGXA200, and DGXA100 nodes carry most of the displayed
schedule, whereas the DGX1 nodes remain off. Because
many high-reward tasks originate in CDC 0, the optimized
solution assigns selected tasks to remote nodes when the
resulting transfer, execution, and site-operation decisions im-
prove the modeled objective. The schedule therefore reflects
the joint formulation; it does not by itself establish a general
performance-per-watt ranking among node types.
5) Cross-CDC Transfer Scheduling: Figure 4 visualizes
the traffic exchanged among the three CDCs and its tempo-
ral evolution. The optimized schedule has a total outbound
transfer volume of 320.62 normalized data units and remotely
executes 39 tasks. The transfer pattern is asymmetric: 14 tasks
move from CDC 0 to CDC 1, 19 from CDC 0 to CDC 2, 5
from CDC 1 to CDC 2, and 1 from CDC 2 to CDC 1. The
solution allocates communication capacity selectively when
remote placement improves the modeled objective. It also
schedules data movement near the corresponding execution
windows while satisfying the modeled inbound and outbound
bandwidth limits. These observations describe how transfer
flexibility is used in this instance without implying that the
same pattern holds for other workloads.
6) Thermal and Air-Conditioning Management: The opti-
mized zone and air-conditioning trajectories remain within the
reported modeled limits throughout the 24-h horizon. Zone
temperatures lie between 24◦C and 27◦C, and the final average
zone temperature of each CDC is 24◦C. AC supply tempera-
tures lie between 24◦C and 25.81◦C. These extrema establish
feasibility with respect to the modeled temperature constraints;
they do not establish robustness to thermal-parameter error or
production safety margins. The result nevertheless illustrates
why node placement and facility operation are evaluated
together: a compute assignment changes the heat input as-
signed to its zone and the corresponding modeled cooling
requirement.
7) Summary of Findings: The comparison identifies com-
plementary effects from the two modeled flexibilities. Re-

Fig. 3. Battery-state trajectories in kWh across the three CDCs for the proposed and baseline scheduling variants.
Fig. 4. Cross-CDC inbound and outbound transfer decisions.
laxing the FIFO-prefix constraint avoids the severe head-
of-line blocking observed in that restricted variant, while
enabling cross-CDC transfer adds 9,541.30 NMU of profit
relative to No TF and expands the feasible placement choices.
The proposed case has the highest completion, concurrency,
utilization, and profit among the three reported solutions while
satisfying the modeled bandwidth and temperature constraints.
For this instance, the results support the potential value of
evaluating computing, communication, and facility decisions
jointly. Broader conclusions require additional workload in-
stances, sensitivity studies, practical scheduling baselines, and
consistent solver-quality records for all variants.
IV. CONCLUSION
This paper used a coupled multi-CDC optimization model to
separate the fixed-instance effects of cross-CDC task transfer
and task-reordering flexibility. Relative to No TF, the proposed
model increases profit by 57.9% and completes 103 rather
than 76 tasks. The more restrictive No TF+FIFO variant
completes 14 tasks and yields negative profit, exposing the
effect of head-of-line blocking under the implemented FIFO-
prefix constraint. The proposed schedule transfers 39 tasks and
satisfies the modeled bandwidth and zone-temperature limits.
These results illustrate the potential value of coordinating com-
puting, communication, and facility operation in the studied
instance. Establishing general performance requires repeated
workload instances, transfer- and energy-parameter sensitiv-
ities, additional scheduling baselines, documented terminal-
storage assumptions, and consistent solver-quality statistics for
all variants.
